resources.string: Connect an Android device over USB to start.
Connect a device in ADB mode to use these tools.
Connect a device in Fastboot mode to use these tools.
Connect a device in Recovery or ADB Sideload mode to use these tools.
No novice/expert permission profiles. No artificial capability gates.
Claiming is exclusive: while the interface is held, no other owner on this host can use it. Nothing is claimed automatically.
Re-examines attached devices and asks for permission again where it is missing.
No device attached. Connect a device over USB.

Protocol mode is unknown until a handshake. Descriptors distinguish an ADB class interface from a Fastboot class one, but not Android from Recovery or Sideload, nor bootloader Fastboot from fastbootd.

A recognised device is connected automatically: the interface is claimed and the ADB handshake runs. The device may ask you to allow debugging from this host. Disconnecting stays in effect until the device is reattached.
Public key sent; waiting for device authorization. Android may show an RSA confirmation dialog.
The connection was lost: %1$s (%2$s). Connect again.
Unknown peer, banner prefix not recognised
Devices have not been examined yet.
The system reports no USB devices at all. Check OTG, the cable and the adapter: without a device there is nothing to ask permission for.
The system reports %1$d USB device(s), but none of them exposes an ADB or Fastboot interface.
This host reports no USB host mode support, so no device can be examined.
The command runs in a non-interactive shell and ends on its own. Output is capped at 64 KiB and the call has a 30 second deadline.
Exit code is unavailable: the device does not support shell,v2.
Line to send to the shell
Opening shell; waiting for the device to confirm the stream…
Closing shell; waiting for the ADB stream to release…
The shell is open and waiting for input.

The shell stays open until you close it. Single commands and file operations keep working meanwhile — each runs on its own stream. Escape sequences are shown as they arrive; they are not interpreted yet.
Path on the device, for example /sdcard/Download/file.zip

Writing creates the file at that path and overwrites whatever is there. The content is generated by the app: choosing your own file needs the artifact source that comes later. On failure the app says what it knows about the file, and "unknown" means exactly that — check it on the device.
Write failed: %1$s. Nothing was written: the request never left this host, so %2$s is untouched.
Write failed: %1$s. The state of %2$s is unknown: the request had already left this host, and the device may hold a partial file. Check it before retrying.
Write reported failure after the device had confirmed it: %1$s (%2$s). This combination should not occur; please report it.
Reading does not save anything: it checks the transfer. Compare the hash with sha256sum on the device — matching hashes prove the bytes arrived intact. Saving to a place you can reach comes later.
Target: empty for system, bootloader, recovery
Accepted: %1$s — the device is going down

Success looks like a disconnect: the device leaves the bus and the link closes. Targets are not restricted — the device knows which ones exist. UNTOUCHED means the request never left the host and retrying is safe; UNKNOWN means it left without confirmation, so do not retry.
Service name, for example shell:ls or sync:
%1$s — accepted, the device left the bus (%2$s)

The service name is passed through as typed; there is no list, because the device knows which services exist. The response size is always named — a service may not answer with text at all, and then the byte count is the only thing known for certain. A reboot: typed here behaves like the reboot button.
Local port, 0 for any free one
Address on the device, for example tcp:5555

Connect to a forward at 127.0.0.1 and its port number, from this phone — the address on the device is never typed into a browser. The listener is bound to loopback and reachable only from this phone; there is no way to open it to the network. The address is passed through as typed — which addresses exist is known by the device. One forward carries up to %1$d connections at a time: behind each are two blocking loops, and the limit is about our threads, not about what may be asked for.
Address the device listens on, for example tcp:7777
Address on this phone, for example tcp:8888

Here the device listens and brings the connections; forwarding above is the other way round. The address on this phone is reached as 127.0.0.1 and its port, so only tcp: works on our side — what to do with other kinds was never observed, and a stream to one of them is refused with a named reason rather than dropped silently. What may be asked of the device is not limited.
Ask the device who it is

Bootloader and fastbootd enumerate through the same interface, so the descriptor cannot tell them apart — only the exchange can. The role is read from is-userspace. When the device does not answer it, the role stays unestablished and is shown as such: operations on dynamic partitions exist in fastbootd and not in the bootloader, and a guess here would break exactly when it is relied upon.
An app-generated pattern for checking byte accounting:
Command, as the device knows it
Sent %2$d s ago, still no answer: %1$s

The exchange frame is lost. The device is still waiting for the bytes of the previous command, so the next one would go nowhere — that is why the lane refuses. Only a fresh claim of the interface clears it. The device itself is not touched and loses nothing.
The list is incomplete: %1$d variables read before the exchange broke off
%1$s was named more than once with different values: %2$s
Lines that could not be parsed: %1$d — kept in the diagnostics

There is no command list here on purpose: what Fastboot offers is known to the device, and a refusal is its answer, not our error. Two things the wire itself cannot carry are named rather than sent silently altered: a command outside ASCII, and one longer than 4096 bytes. The lane is shown because Fastboot has exactly one and losing its framing is sticky — a second command would then go nowhere.
Sent %1$d of %2$d bytes; the device answered %3$s
The device buffer was not touched: not a single byte was sent.
The download buffer now holds something; flashing from it is not safe unless the device confirmed the whole payload.

A button here does not reach the lane on its own: it builds the same string and hands it to the same entry point as the free-form command field, so the engine is one and they have nowhere to diverge. The destructive commands — flash:, erase: and format: — live on the Write tab next to the lock state, because the lock is what decides the form of the warning. The confirmation there is not permission: the command reaches the device unchanged either way. A slot switch can be acknowledged by the device without being made, so the slot is read back separately.
A refusal is the device saying it did not carry the command out. It is not proof that the partition is intact: what is known is what the device said, not what it managed to do before refusing.
%1$s → the device answered OKAY, but %2$s was requested and the device reports %3$s. That does not count as a switch.
%1$s → the device left without answering (%2$d ms). For a reboot that is expected, not a lost link.
What the partition now holds is unknown. It may have been left half-written, and its contents cannot be relied on.
%1$s → the exchange never started: %2$s. The device never saw this command.
A refusal is the device saying the lock is untouched. It is not proof: what is known is what the device said, not what it managed to do before refusing.
The lock state is unknown, and so is the state of user data with it: changing the lock normally wipes the device. This is the worst unknown state Fastboot has.
This will be sent: %1$s. If the device carries it out, the previous contents of the partition are gone and there is nothing here to restore them from.

The lock is confirmed, so the expected outcome is this: the device will almost certainly refuse with FAIL and the partition will not change. On some bootloaders the whole payload is transferred first and the refusal only comes after. The command is sent unchanged regardless — the decision belongs to the device, not to the app.

The confirmation here is not permission: the command reaches the device unchanged either way, only the deliberateness of the tap differs. The confirmation word is asked for only when the lock is confirmed; "unknown" does not count as locked, otherwise not knowing would turn into forbidding. The free-form command field is untouched by all of this and runs the same commands without a prompt. Flashing the buffer sends whatever the download buffer holds right now — if this app put it there, that is a pattern for checking byte accounting, not an image.
fetch: usually lives in fastbootd, not in the bootloader. Sending it from here is allowed — the device answers.
%1$s was NOT read in full: %2$d bytes. This cannot be passed off as the partition — a missing piece is indistinguishable from zeros inside it.
Partitions named: %1$d, confirmed by a substantive field: %2$d. Size, type or the logical flag confirm one; has-slot alone does not — devices answer it for names they do not have.
The plan ran in full: %1$d of %2$d steps
The plan stopped: %1$d of %2$d steps done. The device is left between "before" and "after" — part of it happened, the rest did not.
The package has started reaching the device: there is nothing left to cancel.
Recovery ended the transfer (DONEDONE). This says the host handed everything over, and nothing about the install.
Recovery closed the stream at %1$d%% of confirmed coverage. Nearly complete is not complete.
The stream broke after the package started reaching the device, at %1$d%% of confirmed coverage. The state of the device is unknown whatever that number looks like.
Cancelled before a single byte of the package reached the device.
The device is not answering from Sideload: %1$s
Read the Recovery verdict: only Recovery can say whether it installed.

The content is generated by the app — choosing your own package needs the artifact source that comes later. Everything else is the real path: the same stream, the same block requests, the same acknowledgements. Cancelling is possible only until the first block goes out; after that Recovery may already be changing the device.
Write a file from the device storage…
The provider has no atomic replace: if anything went wrong, check the file before relying on it.
A part-written file was left at the destination — delete it yourself, it looks complete but is not.
The part-written file was removed from the destination.
The file you picked has changed since you picked it: %1$s. Pick it again.
Copying %2$s into the app so blocks can be read in any order: %1$d bytes so far. The device has not been touched.
Recovery asks for blocks in its own order and may ask for the same one twice, so a file that can only be read front to back is copied first. Nothing reaches the device during the copy.
Shows the transfer that is running so the system does not stop it while the app is in the background.

History is kept so that an operation interrupted by the app being killed can be read honestly afterwards — not so that it can be resumed. There is nothing to resume: the transport went away with the process.
Outcome unknown — this is a result, not a missing one.
The package started reaching the device (%1$s), so the state of the device is unknown whatever the percentage looked like. Check it.
Connect to a device over ADB first — the shell runs on it, not here.
%1$d actions. Type a few letters of the one you want.
Nothing matches “%1$s”. Every action is still on its own card below.
How the phone sees your device

Android hands a USB device to one app at a time, and only after you allow it. So NekoFlash first asks the system what is plugged in, then asks you for permission, then holds the interface until you release it. If the list stays empty, the system is not offering the device to any app — that is the phone speaking, not NekoFlash refusing.
Recent commands — tapping one fills the field, it does not send it
Nothing recorded yet in this session.
The last %1$d lines, newest first. The full report is the export above — this pane is here so you can see during a run whether the thing you are testing is being recorded at all.
No operations yet in this install. A long transfer — sideload, a file read or written — appears here while it runs and stays here after it ends, including when it ended with nothing known.
adb … or fastboot … (the prefix may be omitted)
Not implemented yet: %1$s. Nothing was sent.
The plan needs a file, and none was picked. Nothing was sent.
The plan writes a partition: if the device carries it out, the previous contents are gone and there is nothing here to restore them from.
Choose where to save and run
fastboot: download of the picked file (%2$s), then flash:%1$s — one operation
fastboot: download of the picked file (%1$s), then boot
fastboot: fetch:%1$s into a file you choose (%2$s)
adb: the interactive shell below, then %1$s
adb: sideload of the picked archive (%1$s)
adb: the interactive shell below, without a terminal (shell,v2,raw:)
adb: the interactive shell below over the plain shell: service, without an exit code
%1$s: the app answers from its own connection state; nothing is sent to the device
Mode: plain shell: service, no exit code (adb shell -x).
The shell is open in the Terminal section. %1$s
%1$s; an image over %2$d bytes goes in sparse pieces of at most that size
fastboot: set_active to the --slot slot, or to the current one without --slot; not sent if the device does not name it
adb: %1$s into the folder you choose
adb: %1$s as %2$s in the folder you choose
adb: %1$s (a file or folder you pick) to %2$s
adb: %1$s (a file or folder you pick) to %2$s, skipping files with the same time on the device (--sync)
Choose a folder to save into and run
Finished with errors: %1$d files, %2$d bytes, skipped %3$d.
adb: sync %1$s from the folder you pick as the build output: files newer or of another size go to the device
adb: list what sync %1$s would push from the folder you pick, without pushing
. Dry run (-n): the device reads every file and writes nothing
fastboot: flashall from the folder you pick as the build output: android-info.txt requirements, set_active, boot images, then system images, reboot at the end. Options: %1$s
fastboot: update from %1$s (the archive you pick): android-info.txt requirements, set_active, boot images, then system images, reboot at the end. Options: %2$s
fastboot: vendor_boot is read from the device, its ramdisk %1$s is replaced by %2$s (the file you pick), and the image is flashed back; slot: %3$s
fastboot: format %1$s — the phone asks the device for the partition type and size (override: type %2$s, size %3$s), builds an empty file system like mke2fs and flashes it. Options: %4$s
fastboot: -w — erase and a fresh file system for userdata, cache and metadata (a partition the device does not know is skipped), then: %1$s. Options: %2$s
fastboot: wipe-super from %1$s (the file you pick): an empty super built from its metadata is flashed to each super device; slot: %2$s

The same engines run this as the buttons and the raw console. A path in the command is never opened directly: the file is picked through Android and bound to the plan shown above. A command or option without an executor answers \"not implemented\" before anything is sent, instead of turning into a different command. `flash` of an image larger than the device\'s max-download-size goes in sparse pieces, as with desktop fastboot.
The command names %1$d files, and %2$d were picked. Nothing was sent.
adb: install of the picked package (%1$s), package flags: %2$s
adb: install session for the picked packages (%1$s), package flags: %2$s
Installed: %1$d file(s), %2$d bytes. The device answered: %3$s
Not installed: %1$d file(s), %2$d bytes sent. The device answered: %3$s
The installation did not reach the device\'s answer: %1$s
%1$s — slot %2$s, checked against slot-count; a partition gets the suffix only if has-slot answers yes
%1$s — a partition whose has-slot answers yes gets the current slot suffix, as with desktop fastboot
%1$s; the vbmeta header gets %2$s before the first byte
